messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Counselor
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 46

She calls it the second, though she knows it was less than one. The exact number doesn’t matter; it lives inside her like a clock that never stops ticking. She was driving home from a long day at the community mental health center, her mind still humming with a client’s story about childhood neglect. The light was green, the sun low and golden. A man stepped off the curb into the crosswalk—not running, just walking, like he had all the time in the world. She looked down for a moment to adjust the radio volume, and when she looked up he was there, right in front of her. The thud. The scream from her own throat that she didn’t recognize.

He survived. That’s what she tells herself every morning, as if the word “survived” can erase the image of his leg bent at an angle that legs should never bend, the sound of the paramedic shouting for a backboard. He survived, but he will never walk the same way again. She knows this because his lawyer sent a letter, and because she found his name online, and because she knows—with the precise clinical knowledge of a trained counselor—that the word “survived” does not mean “unharmed.”

Now, eight months later, she sits in her office across from a young woman who is crying about a recent breakup, and she cannot feel a thing. She nods, murmurs the right empathic phrases, but inside there is only a flat gray static. She has become a machine that says the right words without meaning them. Her clients do not notice—they are too wrapped up in their own pain—but she notices. She notices that she stopped taking the route that passes the intersection, even though it adds twenty minutes to her commute. She notices that she flinches every time a car horn sounds outside the window. She notices that her hands shake when she reaches for her keys.

At night, she lies awake next to her husband, replaying the moment over and over, trying to find the place where she could have turned left instead of right, or braked a second sooner. He reaches for her in the dark and she stiffens, not because she doesn’t love him but because touch feels like too much. She is afraid that if she lets herself feel his warmth, she will also feel the cold shock of that impact again. She has started avoiding sex, avoiding conversation about the future, avoiding any topic that might lead to a question like “Do you want to drive tonight?” She says she’s tired. She is always tired.

On the weekends, she stays inside. The thought of getting behind the wheel makes her stomach drop. She takes the bus to work, sitting in the back with her eyes closed, counting the stops. She knows this is avoidance. She knows the cognitive-behavioral worksheets by heart—she has given them to dozens of clients. But knowing and doing are two different rooms, and she is locked in the first one.

The other day, a client mentioned a car accident during session, and she felt her vision tunnel, her jaw clench. She had to excuse herself to the bathroom and breathe into her cupped hands. When she came back, she apologized and said she had a headache. The client believed her. That’s the worst part—they always believe her. She is so good at pretending to be okay that she has almost convinced herself. But the PCL-5 she filled out last week for her own therapist (she finally saw someone, because she knows the research, knows the prognosis if left untreated) came to 46. She knows what that number means. She sat in her car—her husband’s car, since she can’t drive hers anymore—and stared at the total for a long time, feeling nothing at all.

Sometimes, when she is alone, she whispers the man’s name into the dark. She found it in the police report. She says it over and over until it becomes just a sound, a string of syllables that no longer belongs to a real person. But it always does. It always goes back to belonging to a real person, a person whose life she changed in a single second that she will never get back. She watches the clock on her nightstand click forward. She waits for morning.
